name: Enlicitide
summary: Enlicitide is an oral PCSK9 inhibitor approved by the FDA in July 2026 to lower LDL cholesterol in adults with hypercholesterolemia, including heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. It is a peptide cholesterol medicine, not a GLP-1 drug or an obesity treatment.
description: Marketed as Lipfendra, enlicitide represents an oral approach to a target previously addressed principally through injectable therapies. Its approval is for LDL-cholesterol reduction alongside diet and exercise in adults. The CORALreef program demonstrated large lipid reductions, including in patients already receiving other lipid-lowering care. However, a trial whose primary endpoint is LDL change does not by itself prove a specific reduction in heart attacks or strokes for this molecule. The catalog therefore distinguishes established LDL-lowering efficacy from the separate question of drug-specific cardiovascular-outcome evidence.
mechanism: PCSK9 normally promotes degradation of LDL receptors after they bind circulating LDL particles. Enlicitide blocks the interaction between PCSK9 and the LDL receptor, allowing more receptors to return to the liver-cell surface and remove LDL from blood. Its macrocyclic peptide design and oral formulation make delivery possible despite the absorption challenges typical of peptides. Food-related administration requirements are formulation-specific.
keyTakeaway: Enlicitide’s status changed from investigational to FDA approved in July 2026. Its established role is LDL lowering; broader cardiovascular claims should remain tied to the actual outcomes evidence and current label.

sections.title: Approved scope
sections.body: Lipfendra is approved as an adjunct to diet and exercise to reduce LDL-C in adults with hypercholesterolemia, including heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. The indication is not weight loss and does not establish pediatric use.

sections.title: CORALreef Lipids
sections.body: The randomized trial included 2,909 participants in its intention-to-treat population. At twenty-four weeks, enlicitide produced an adjusted LDL-C reduction about 55.8 percentage points greater than placebo, with reductions maintained at the later study assessment.

sections.title: Lipid endpoints and clinical outcomes
sections.body: Lower LDL-C is a well-established therapeutic target, but this trial primarily measured lipids. The label discusses cardiovascular-outcome evidence for statins and monoclonal-antibody PCSK9 inhibitors; that should not be rewritten as a completed enlicitide-specific cardiovascular-outcome trial.

sections.title: Adverse effects and remaining questions
sections.body: Overall adverse-event frequencies were similar to placebo in the major hypercholesterolemia trial. Diarrhea and dizziness were the most common label-listed adverse reactions in the HeFH study. Human pregnancy and lactation data are limited, and the label addresses potential fetal concerns from cholesterol lowering.

sections.title: How follow-up is judged
sections.body: Response is assessed with LDL-C and the person’s overall lipid-management plan. An oral route may alter treatment preferences, but it does not make enlicitide interchangeable with statins, antibody PCSK9 inhibitors or other lipid therapies on a milligram basis.

name: Glepaglutide
summary: Glepaglutide is an investigational GLP-2 analog for short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure. Phase 3 evidence supports reduced parenteral-support needs with one studied regimen, while another did not meet efficacy endpoints; a second pivotal program is underway.
description: The treatment is designed for people whose remaining intestine cannot absorb enough fluid or nutrients without intravenous support. In the EASE-1 study, glepaglutide was tested at two administration frequencies against placebo. The positive results were regimen-specific, an important qualification that disappears in simple claims that the molecule 'worked in phase 3.' The sponsor reports that the EASE-5 confirmatory study began recruiting in January 2026 after a U.S. complete response letter. Current sponsor information explicitly describes glepaglutide as investigational and not approved by FDA or any other health authority.
mechanism: Glepaglutide activates GLP-2 receptors to promote intestinal adaptation and increase absorption. Its long-acting design is intended to sustain that response with less frequent administration than daily GLP-2 therapy. Changes in absorptive capacity can alter the balance between oral intake, intestinal losses and parenteral support. The clinical aim is a safe reduction in support, not intestinal growth as an isolated laboratory endpoint.
keyTakeaway: Glepaglutide has meaningful but regimen-specific phase 3 findings and remains unapproved. Confirmatory evidence, durability and specialist management of fluid and nutritional needs remain central to its development.

sections.title: The intended clinical problem
sections.body: Patients in the pivotal study required parenteral support on at least three days per week. The program addresses intestinal failure after loss of bowel, rather than ordinary constipation, IBS or a general wish to improve intestinal permeability.

sections.title: What EASE-1 demonstrated
sections.body: Among 106 randomized and treated patients, the twice-weekly trial regimen reduced support volume more than placebo at twenty-four weeks. About 14% in that group achieved complete support independence. The once-weekly regimen did not show significant superiority on primary or key secondary endpoints.

sections.title: Why study regimen matters
sections.body: The efficacy difference between regimens means that one cannot assume every exposure schedule produces the same result. Enteral autonomy in a minority of participants also should not be described as a guaranteed outcome for all patients with short bowel syndrome.

sections.title: Long-term assessment
sections.body: EASE-1 reported generally favorable tolerability, but its size and duration do not settle uncommon or delayed risks. Continued development evaluates sustained support reduction and safety over longer treatment, including the consequences of improved absorption and intestinal trophic activity.

sections.title: Current development status
sections.body: The sponsor’s current pipeline page describes EASE-5 as a second pivotal phase 3 study recruiting in Europe and the United States from January 2026. It explicitly states that glepaglutide is investigational and not approved by any health authority.

name: Larazotide acetate
summary: Larazotide acetate is an investigational intestinal-barrier peptide studied chiefly as an adjunct to a gluten-free diet in celiac disease. Early symptom results were mixed, and its pivotal celiac program was discontinued; it is not an approved way to make gluten exposure safe.
description: Also known as AT-1001 or INN-202, larazotide was developed to influence epithelial tight junctions, the structures that help control movement between intestinal cells. A randomized phase 2 study enrolled adults with persistent celiac symptoms despite a gluten-free diet. Only the lowest studied group met the primary symptom endpoint, while higher groups did not. The subsequent phase 3 celiac program did not deliver an approval and was discontinued in 2022. Other investigational interest does not reverse that evidence history or validate broad claims about treating an undefined 'leaky gut' syndrome.
mechanism: Larazotide is intended to regulate tight-junction behavior and reduce excessive paracellular permeability. Development research links its activity to pathways involved in gliadin-associated barrier disruption rather than directly digesting gluten or eliminating celiac autoimmunity. The mechanism is biologically plausible but does not establish that treated patients can safely abandon dietary avoidance, nor that all gastrointestinal symptoms arise from the same barrier defect.
keyTakeaway: Larazotide has human research history but no established celiac treatment role. Mixed early findings and a discontinued pivotal program should be included whenever its intestinal-barrier mechanism is discussed.

sections.title: The question studied in celiac disease
sections.body: The phase 2 trial studied persistent symptoms in adults already following a gluten-free diet for at least a year. Participants continued that diet. It was an adjunct-treatment study, not a demonstration that larazotide could replace dietary management.

sections.title: Mixed dose-group results
sections.body: Among 342 randomized adults, the lowest studied group improved the prespecified gastrointestinal symptom score compared with placebo. The two higher groups did not differ from placebo. This nonuniform result limits a simple claim of proven efficacy across exposures.

sections.title: What happened to phase 3
sections.body: A 2022 SEC filing reports the decision to discontinue further development of larazotide in celiac disease. The later-stage program therefore cannot be cited as successful confirmation of the earlier symptom findings.

sections.title: What early tolerability can establish
sections.body: Adverse-event findings in the phase 2 study were broadly comparable with placebo. That supports the tolerability assessment of that study, but does not establish long-term safety in all populations or safety of unverified products sold for unrelated indications.

sections.title: Does it permit gluten consumption?
sections.body: The evidence does not establish protection from celiac injury during unrestricted gluten exposure. Symptom improvement, intestinal permeability and mucosal disease control are distinct endpoints. A quieter digestive tract would not by itself prove that celiac inflammation is controlled.

name: Mazdutide
molecularClass: Dual GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist peptide
summary: Mazdutide is a dual GLP-1/glucagon agonist approved in China for weight management and type 2 diabetes. It has randomized clinical evidence, but Chinese authorization should not be confused with FDA approval or identical eligibility and availability in other countries.
description: Developed as IBI362 and LY3305677, mazdutide combines appetite-related incretin signaling with glucagon receptor activity. Innovent announced China’s first approval for weight management in June 2025 and a subsequent type 2 diabetes approval that year. The GLORY-1 obesity trial enrolled Chinese adults using locally relevant BMI thresholds. That population and regulatory context matter when interpreting the results internationally. This catalog records the medicine as approved in its actual jurisdiction, while preserving the distinction between an NMPA-authorized product and an unapproved import or research preparation elsewhere.
mechanism: GLP-1 receptor activation supports glucose-dependent insulin secretion, reduced food intake and other metabolic effects. Glucagon receptor activation adds effects on hepatic metabolism and energy expenditure, with the combined molecule designed to balance glucose and weight responses. The two targets distinguish mazdutide from GLP-1-only medicines and from GIP/GLP-1 agonists. Target count alone does not establish comparative effectiveness or safety.
keyTakeaway: Mazdutide is an approved Chinese metabolic medicine with phase 3 evidence, not a universally approved peptide. Its jurisdiction, exact indication and studied population must accompany any benefit claim.

sections.title: Chinese approval scope
sections.body: Innovent’s official announcements document NMPA approval for chronic weight management in June 2025 and for type 2 diabetes later in 2025. These authorizations concern regulated products and locally defined eligibility.

sections.title: GLORY-1 trial
sections.body: The phase 3 study randomized 610 Chinese adults with obesity or qualifying overweight. At forty-eight weeks, the higher trial group had a mean weight change of −14.01%, compared with +0.30% with placebo. The study also assessed cardiometabolic measures.

sections.title: What the trial reported
sections.body: Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequent and were mostly mild or moderate. Low discontinuation rates in this particular trial do not eliminate uncommon risks or show that tolerability will match in every clinical population.

sections.title: Population and endpoint boundaries
sections.body: The trial’s BMI thresholds, baseline characteristics and background care differ from many North American or European obesity trials. Indirect percentage comparisons do not establish superiority. Weight and risk-factor changes also do not substitute for a completed cardiovascular-outcomes study.

sections.title: Why approval location matters
sections.body: A medicine can be approved in China while remaining unapproved by the FDA. The applicable product information, manufacturing source and prescribing rules follow the jurisdiction, and foreign approval does not validate an online seller’s version of the ingredient.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.body:
Is mazdutide approved everywhere? No. The cited approvals are in China; they do not authorize marketing in the United States.

Does the Chinese obesity trial establish the same response in every population? No. GLORY-1 provides direct evidence in its enrolled Chinese population, while generalization to other groups, clinical settings and long-term outcomes requires additional evidence.

name: Pemvidutide
molecularClass: Dual GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist peptide
summary: Pemvidutide is an investigational metabolic peptide studied for obesity and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis. In a phase 2b MASH trial, it improved the inflammation-resolution endpoint at twenty-four weeks but did not significantly improve the separate fibrosis endpoint at that time.
description: Pemvidutide, formerly ALT-801, is designed to combine GLP-1 and glucagon receptor activity. Its liver program distinguishes fat reduction, resolution of steatohepatitis and improvement in scarring because these are related but different outcomes. IMPACT enrolled patients with biopsy-confirmed MASH and moderate-to-advanced fibrosis. The published interim analysis supports activity against MASH, while the negative fibrosis comparison remains important. Marketing language that says a peptide 'reverses fatty liver' can obscure these distinctions, the investigational status and the need for longer follow-up to evaluate clinical consequences.
mechanism: GLP-1 signaling influences appetite and glucose regulation, while glucagon receptor activity changes hepatic metabolism and can increase energy expenditure. The combined design aims to reduce body weight and liver fat without losing glycemic control. Reduced hepatic fat may contribute to improvement in inflammation, but remodeling established fibrosis is a separate biological process and must be measured directly rather than assumed from weight loss.
keyTakeaway: Pemvidutide has promising human MASH evidence with a clearly mixed endpoint result. It remains investigational, and improvement in liver inflammation should not be described as established reversal of fibrosis or cirrhosis.

sections.title: Who was studied
sections.body: IMPACT enrolled 212 patients with biopsy-confirmed MASH and stage F2 or F3 fibrosis. It did not establish treatment for all causes of elevated liver enzymes, all degrees of fibrosis or decompensated cirrhosis.

sections.title: Positive MASH endpoint
sections.body: At twenty-four weeks, MASH resolution without worsening fibrosis occurred in 58% and 52% of the two active groups versus 20% with placebo. The prespecified analysis supported a treatment effect on that endpoint.

sections.title: Fibrosis result was different
sections.body: Fibrosis improvement without worsening MASH occurred in 33% and 36% of the active groups versus 28% with placebo; neither comparison was statistically significant. The study therefore did not meet both primary endpoints at the reported time point.

sections.title: Tolerability and remaining uncertainty
sections.body: Most adverse events were mild or moderate, and discontinuation because of adverse events was uncommon in the reported study. Longer exposure and larger populations remain necessary to characterize rare harms and the clinical importance of histologic changes.

sections.title: Why several liver measures are needed
sections.body: Body weight, imaging-derived liver fat, liver enzymes, inflammation and fibrosis answer different questions. Earlier metabolic studies support development, but a favorable change in one measure cannot be substituted for proven reduction in liver failure, transplantation or mortality.

name: Petrelintide
summary: Petrelintide is an investigational amylin analog for obesity with positive phase 2 results. It targets appetite through a pathway different from GLP-1-only medicines, but its weight-loss, gastrointestinal tolerability and long-term outcome evidence are still developing.
description: Formerly ZP8396, petrelintide is being developed by Zealand Pharma and Roche as a long-acting amylin-based obesity treatment. The ZUPREME-1 study evaluated adults without type 2 diabetes over forty-two weeks, while other studies address diabetes and potential combinations. The program is clinically substantive, but a phase 2 result does not establish the full benefit-risk profile or imply that every amylin analog behaves alike. In particular, petrelintide, cagrilintide and pramlintide differ in molecule, duration, formulation and approved or investigational purpose, so their evidence should not be pooled into one product claim.
mechanism: Amylin is a pancreatic peptide involved in satiation and meal-related regulation. Petrelintide is engineered to extend amylin-related receptor signaling and reduce food intake with prolonged exposure. This mechanism offers a route to appetite regulation that does not require GLP-1 agonism in the same molecule. Clinical trials are needed to determine whether the design produces a useful balance of weight reduction and tolerability.
keyTakeaway: Petrelintide has encouraging phase 2 obesity evidence, including a potentially useful tolerability profile, but remains investigational. Comparisons with established medicines require direct studies and a fuller long-term safety record.

sections.title: Development population
sections.body: ZUPREME-1 enrolled adults with obesity or qualifying overweight without type 2 diabetes. Separate development addresses adults with diabetes and combinations. These populations should remain distinct when presenting expected outcomes.

sections.title: Phase 2 weight results
sections.body: The study randomized 493 participants, with 485 exposed to treatment. Mean weight reduction continued through forty-two weeks, reaching up to 10.7% in the reported efficacy analysis. The analysis assumed a particular treatment-adherence scenario rather than predicting every real-world outcome.

sections.title: What favorable tolerability means
sections.body: Nausea was more frequent with petrelintide than placebo; vomiting was uncommon, and diarrhea and constipation rates were relatively similar. This is an encouraging study-specific pattern, not evidence of no gastrointestinal effects or proof of superiority to another agent.

sections.title: Questions phase 2 cannot settle
sections.body: The trial was not designed to establish reductions in cardiovascular events or mortality. Longer-term persistence, uncommon harms and effects in more diverse populations remain relevant, even when average weight reduction and short-term tolerability look favorable.

sections.title: Next-stage interpretation
sections.body: Roche and Zealand describe continued development, including plans for later-stage studies and combinations. Company announcements are useful for program status but should be identified separately from peer-reviewed clinical findings and final regulatory decisions.

name: PN-943
molecularClass: Oral gastrointestinal-restricted α4β7 integrin antagonist peptide
summary: PN-943 is an investigational oral peptide designed to block gut-directed immune-cell trafficking in ulcerative colitis. Its phase 2 study missed the prespecified primary endpoint, with an exploratory signal at the lower exposure; it is distinct from predecessor PTG-100.
description: The development concept is local intestinal activity with low systemic exposure. PN-943 binds α4β7 integrin, a target also used by an approved antibody medicine, but that shared target does not establish equivalent efficacy or safety. Healthy-volunteer studies supported oral stability and target engagement. The IDEAL phase 2 study then tested clinical remission in moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis. Its higher-exposure primary comparison was negative, while the lower group showed a numerical signal. The sponsor subsequently prioritized other programs and stated that it would not commit further internal development resources beyond completing the extension.
mechanism: α4β7 integrin helps leukocytes interact with MAdCAM-1 and traffic to intestinal tissue. PN-943 is designed to inhibit that interaction and related immune-cell activation while remaining largely within the gastrointestinal compartment. Low measured plasma exposure is consistent with this design, but it does not by itself prove adequate tissue effect or absence of systemic biological consequences. Receptor occupancy is a pharmacodynamic marker, not clinical remission.
keyTakeaway: PN-943 provides proof-of-concept research for an oral gut-restricted approach, with a mixed clinical result and an inactive internal development commitment. It should not be described as approved oral vedolizumab or merged with PTG-100.

sections.title: What healthy-volunteer studies showed
sections.body: Phase 1 studies found low systemic exposure and measurable target engagement, with generally favorable short-term tolerability. These findings supported testing in ulcerative colitis but could not establish clinical efficacy in inflamed bowel.

sections.title: IDEAL results
sections.body: The sponsor reported 159 evaluable patients. The higher trial group did not separate from placebo on the prespecified primary endpoint. The lower group had 27.5% clinical remission versus 14.5% with placebo, a numerical difference that did not reach conventional statistical significance in the overall analysis.

sections.title: Do not substitute a predecessor study
sections.body: PTG-100 is a related predecessor, not another name for PN-943. Results from PTG-100 cannot be assigned directly to PN-943. Similarly, efficacy of an approved injectable α4β7 antibody validates the target’s relevance without validating this oral molecule.

sections.title: What remains unresolved
sections.body: Early tolerability and low plasma exposure do not establish long-term safety in active inflammatory bowel disease, combination therapy or pregnancy. A complete clinical benefit-risk profile would require successful confirmatory development and broader exposure.

sections.title: Program status
sections.body: In its third-quarter 2022 update, Protagonist stated that it intended to dedicate no further internal clinical or manufacturing-development resources after completing the IDEAL extension. The record is therefore research history, not evidence of an approved or continuously advancing phase 3 product.

name: Survodutide
molecularClass: Dual glucagon and GLP-1 receptor agonist peptide
summary: Survodutide is an investigational dual glucagon/GLP-1 agonist with clinical programs in obesity and MASH. Phase 2 liver and phase 3 obesity findings support further development, while gastrointestinal tolerability and the distinction between weight, inflammation and fibrosis outcomes remain important.
description: Known during development as BI 456906, survodutide combines two receptor activities in a long-acting peptide. Its development includes obesity trials in people with and without diabetes and liver studies in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis. SYNCHRONIZE-1 results reported in 2026 provide phase 3 obesity evidence, moving beyond the earlier proof-of-concept studies. That progress does not itself establish marketing approval. The liver and obesity programs also answer separate questions: a reduction in body weight or liver fat is not automatically proof of improved fibrosis, prevention of cirrhosis or fewer cardiovascular events.
mechanism: GLP-1 receptor activity affects appetite, glucose-dependent insulin secretion and gastric emptying. Glucagon receptor activity adds hepatic and energy-expenditure effects. Survodutide’s design seeks to combine these actions into useful weight and liver responses while balancing glucose regulation. Because receptor balance, exposure and patient population differ among dual agonists, findings for another GLP-1/glucagon peptide cannot substitute for survodutide-specific trials.
keyTakeaway: Survodutide has advanced clinical evidence for obesity and MASH but remained investigational at this review. Benefits should be stated for the specific trial endpoint, with tolerability and long-term clinical uncertainty included.

sections.title: Distinct development programs
sections.body: Obesity studies assess weight change and related outcomes, while MASH studies evaluate liver disease directly. Eligibility and background disease differ, so the programs should not be combined into a single undifferentiated metabolic-benefit claim.

sections.title: MASH phase 2 findings
sections.body: A randomized liver trial found greater improvement in MASH without worsening fibrosis with survodutide than placebo. This supports activity on the prespecified histologic endpoint; it does not by itself demonstrate prevention of liver failure or a survival benefit.

sections.title: Phase 3 obesity evidence
sections.body: The 2026 SYNCHRONIZE-1 report describes greater body-weight reduction than placebo in adults with obesity without diabetes. The published study and sponsor announcement should be interpreted using their specified analysis and population, rather than informal cross-trial rankings.

sections.title: Tolerability considerations
sections.body: Gastrointestinal adverse events were prominent in clinical development. Treatment discontinuation and exposure escalation affect both tolerability and reported efficacy. Larger studies and follow-up are needed to clarify uncommon risks and long-term use in patients with multiple comorbidities.

sections.title: What remains to be established
sections.body: Positive late-stage results are part of an approval submission, not a final authorization. At this review date, survodutide is retained as investigational; the evidence does not validate a research supplier’s product or a self-directed combination with other metabolic medicines.

name: BPC-157
summary: BPC-157 is a synthetic fifteen-amino-acid peptide studied mainly in laboratory and animal models of injury and gastrointestinal inflammation. Human evidence is limited and methodologically weak, and FDA review has not established a clinical safety or effectiveness profile for the promoted uses.
description: BPC-157 is also called bepecin or PL-14736. It attracts interest for tendon, muscle and gastrointestinal recovery, but the volume of animal publications should not be mistaken for a large body of reliable human trials. FDA’s 2026 evaluation identified small human reports, a limited ulcerative-colitis meeting abstract and substantial gaps in route-specific safety. A registered healthy-volunteer study does not supply a usable efficacy result merely because it appears in a trial registry. Claims that the molecule universally heals tissues go well beyond the available controlled human evidence.
mechanism: Preclinical studies report effects on cell migration, stress survival and tissue-repair signaling. In rat tendon-cell experiments, BPC-157 altered FAK–paxillin signaling and fibroblast outgrowth; these are mechanistic findings in experimental tissue, not a validated human receptor-based treatment model. Different injury systems and routes can produce different exposures, so an observed laboratory pathway does not establish a safe or effective clinical regimen.
keyTakeaway: BPC-157 has research interest but insufficient high-quality human evidence for routine healing claims. Evolving compounding discussions are separate from FDA drug approval and do not supply the missing clinical evidence.

sections.title: What laboratory research supports
sections.body: A tendon study found improved fibroblast migration, outgrowth and survival under experimental stress, alongside activation of FAK and paxillin. These results identify hypotheses for further investigation; they do not demonstrate faster return to sport or durable tendon healing in patients.

sections.title: What the human record can establish
sections.body: FDA’s 2026 assessment found that the small ulcerative-colitis evidence was insufficient for an effectiveness conclusion and that human safety information could not adequately characterize the proposed products. Small uncontrolled reports cannot separate treatment effects from natural recovery or concurrent care.

sections.title: Known gaps and plausible product risks
sections.body: The absence of a well-defined adverse-event rate is a gap, not reassurance. FDA highlighted uncertainty about immune reactions, peptide-related impurities and characterization. Sterility, composition and exposure also differ between proposed oral, local and injectable products.

sections.title: Compounding review is not approval
sections.body: BPC-157 was considered in the 2026 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee process. Such review concerns compounding policy and does not establish approval of a drug as safe and effective. This record therefore avoids treating an advisory development as an approved therapeutic indication.

sections.title: Is BPC-157 the same as TB-500?
sections.body: No. They are different substances with different sequences and evidence. A combination marketed under a recovery nickname does not establish the benefit or safety of either component, and findings for one cannot be assigned to the other.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.body:
Do animal tendon findings prove faster recovery in people? No. Tendon-cell and animal experiments establish research hypotheses; they do not measure reliable clinical healing, return to sport or long-term human safety.

Does a compounding advisory discussion approve BPC-157? No. FDA's review of bulk substances and any advisory recommendation are separate from approval of a finished medicine for a specific indication.

name: KPV
summary: KPV is a three-amino-acid fragment associated with α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone research. It has shown anti-inflammatory activity in mouse colitis and cell-delivery experiments, but these findings have not established an effective, safe treatment for human inflammatory bowel disease or skin conditions.
description: The name KPV describes the amino-acid sequence lysine, proline and valine. Research focuses on whether this small peptide can influence inflammatory signaling while avoiding some effects of the full parent hormone. Two important distinctions are the biological model and the delivery system: a mouse receiving a specially engineered nanoparticle formulation is not equivalent to a person taking a commercially sold capsule or injection. The 2026 FDA compounding review addresses the lack of an established human product profile. This catalog includes the research without presenting it as approved gut repair.
mechanism: KPV has reduced inflammatory readouts in experimental systems, including models of colitis. Some effects appear partly independent of melanocortin-1 receptor signaling, so it should not be described simply as a miniature version of every α-MSH action. Delivery to intestinal epithelial cells and macrophages is a major research issue. Nanoparticle targeting can change tissue exposure and therefore is part of the intervention, not a neutral packaging detail.
keyTakeaway: KPV’s evidence is preclinical and formulation-dependent. Mouse inflammation findings justify investigation, but do not establish human efficacy, a standard clinical route or a known long-term safety margin.

sections.title: Animal colitis findings
sections.body: An original study found improvement in inflammatory measures in two mouse colitis models. Experiments in animals with impaired MC1 receptor function suggested that at least part of the response did not require that receptor.

sections.title: Why formulation changes the evidence
sections.body: A later study loaded KPV into hyaluronic-acid-functionalized nanoparticles within a hydrogel. This improved targeted delivery and mouse colitis outcomes relative to comparison systems. It does not establish equivalent activity for unformulated oral KPV or injected products.

sections.title: What has not been demonstrated
sections.body: These studies do not establish remission, prevention of complications or improved quality of life in people with ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease. Histologic improvement in a chemically induced mouse model is a different endpoint from sustained human disease control.

sections.title: The human safety gap
sections.body: FDA’s 2026 assessment considered inadequate human exposure and safety information among the key concerns. A small peptide can still have uncertain immune, impurity and formulation-related risks; absence of documented reactions in a limited literature is not proof of safety.

sections.title: What regulatory discussion means
sections.body: KPV-related bulk substances were reviewed for possible compounding use in 2026. A compounding-policy discussion does not create an FDA-approved KPV drug or demonstrate that a particular commercial formulation treats inflammatory disease.

name: AOD-9604
summary: AOD-9604 is a modified growth-hormone fragment investigated for obesity. Animal fat-metabolism findings did not translate into convincing human weight-loss efficacy, and a large clinical program was discontinued. It is not an FDA-approved obesity medicine or full-length growth-hormone replacement.
description: AOD-9604 consists of a tyrosine added to the 177–191 region of human growth hormone. That defined modified sequence matters because commercial descriptions often blur it with native Fragment 176–191. Early rodent work suggested effects on fat metabolism without the full growth-hormone receptor profile. Human obesity development subsequently failed to show adequate benefit over placebo in the large OPTIONS study. The molecule remains scientifically interesting, but that history should accompany claims about targeted fat loss rather than being replaced by selected positive animal results or unsupported claims of selective abdominal-fat reduction.
mechanism: Preclinical studies examined reduced lipogenesis, increased fat oxidation and lipolysis. One mouse and cell study found that AOD-9604 did not compete for the growth-hormone receptor or stimulate receptor-dependent proliferation in the tested system. This distinguishes it mechanistically from intact GH, but does not prove complete absence of endocrine or other effects in humans. A reliably validated human fat-loss mechanism has not emerged from the negative efficacy program.
keyTakeaway: AOD-9604 has a defined research identity and negative major obesity-trial history. It should not be presented as proven fat loss without GH-related risks, or automatically merged with every product labeled Fragment 176–191.

atAGlance.value: Large trial did not beat placebo

sections.title: What animal studies found
sections.body: Studies in obese rats and mice reported altered fat metabolism and reduced weight gain. The tested species, exposure and outcome matter: reducing weight gain in an animal model is not the same as producing clinically useful weight loss in adults.

sections.title: The important negative trial
sections.body: FDA’s review describes the OPTIONS study, which enrolled 536 adults and found no significant weight-loss difference from placebo. The developer ended obesity development after that result. This is central evidence, not a minor omission from an otherwise proven treatment.

sections.title: Relationship to Fragment 176–191
sections.body: The analytical literature defines AOD-9604 as hGH 177–191 with an added N-terminal tyrosine. Native fragment nomenclature is not an assurance of that same sequence. Molecular identity must be established before evidence can be transferred between names.

sections.title: What safety claims cannot establish
sections.body: A lack of selected GH-like effects in preclinical experiments does not provide a complete human safety profile. Long-term use, injected preparations, immune responses and product purity require evidence specific to the formulation and route.

sections.title: Current clinical meaning
sections.body: AOD-9604 is not an FDA-approved drug for obesity. A compounding discussion, ingredient listing or food-related safety claim is not approval of an injectable weight-loss medicine and does not overturn the unsuccessful obesity efficacy evidence.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.body:
Did AOD-9604 demonstrate meaningful weight loss in its major obesity trial? FDA's review describes a large trial without statistically significant weight loss versus placebo. Animal metabolic findings do not overturn that result.

Is every vial called Fragment 176–191 chemically equivalent? No. AOD-9604 has a defined modified sequence; vendor shorthand alone cannot establish the identity or purity of another material.

name: 5-Amino-1MQ
summary: 5-Amino-1MQ is a small-molecule inhibitor of nicotinamide N-methyltransferase, not a peptide. Mouse and cell studies report metabolic effects, but they do not establish effective human weight loss, improved longevity or a validated safety profile for commercial products.
description: Also written 5A1MQ or 5-amino-1-methylquinolinium, this compound is included because it appears in peptide-oriented catalogs despite its different chemistry. The experimental target, NNMT, participates in nicotinamide methylation and links to cellular energy and methyl-donor metabolism. Original studies used cultured adipocytes and diet-induced obese mice, with later work examining liver and metabolic outcomes. These findings support target investigation. They do not establish that blocking NNMT is beneficial in every tissue or that self-administered oral or injectable preparations reproduce the exposure achieved in controlled animal experiments.
mechanism: NNMT converts nicotinamide to 1-methylnicotinamide using S-adenosylmethionine as a methyl donor. Inhibiting it can change intracellular nicotinamide-related metabolites, NAD-associated pathways and methyl-donor availability. Experimental 5-amino-1MQ studies connect those changes to reduced lipogenesis and altered energy handling. NNMT has tissue-specific functions, so a proposed metabolic benefit cannot be reduced to the claim that raising NAD is automatically beneficial throughout the body.
keyTakeaway: 5-Amino-1MQ is a preclinical small molecule, not an established peptide therapy. Its animal findings and target biology warrant research but do not provide human efficacy, interaction or long-term safety evidence.

sections.title: Early metabolic experiments
sections.body: The original inhibitor study found reduced lipogenesis in cultured adipocytes and lower body weight and adipose mass in obese mice. The authors linked effects to changes in metabolic regulators, but did not establish a human weight-management treatment.

sections.title: Later obesity and liver findings
sections.body: A 2024 mouse study reported improvements in glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity and liver fat-related pathology, alongside pharmacokinetic and tissue-distribution work. These are preclinical outcomes and should not be described as demonstrated reversal of human MASH.

sections.title: Why a target is not a treatment
sections.body: A compound can inhibit the intended enzyme yet have inadequate exposure, off-target activity or an unfavorable safety margin in people. Dose-response and tissue-distribution data from mice do not supply a clinically validated human regimen.

sections.title: Human uncertainty
sections.body: The cited research does not establish adverse-event frequencies, reproductive safety, long-term toxicity or drug interactions in humans. Short animal studies with no obvious toxicity cannot answer those questions. Product identity and purity add separate uncertainties outside regulated development.

sections.title: Why it is labeled nonpeptide
sections.body: Its methylquinolinium scaffold is not an amino-acid chain. Keeping that distinction visible prevents readers from assuming it shares the pharmacology, manufacturing requirements or clinical evidence of approved peptide medicines merely because sellers group them together.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.body:
Is 5-Amino-1MQ actually a peptide? No. It is a small-molecule NNMT inhibitor and is included here because it appears in the reference catalog.

Have its animal weight and liver findings been established in patients? The cited studies are preclinical. They do not establish a human clinical benefit, a safe treatment regimen or a replacement for approved obesity or liver-disease care.

name: Fragment 176-191
molecularClass: C-terminal growth-hormone fragment; product identity requires verification
summary: Fragment 176–191 refers to a C-terminal region of human growth hormone, but commercial naming is inconsistent and often overlaps with the modified peptide AOD-9604. Evidence from neighboring fragments cannot establish human fat-loss efficacy for an unspecified product carrying this label.
description: A native amino-acid fragment, a modified analog and a supplier’s trade label are different forms of identification. The older literature studied hGH 177–191, while AOD-9604 has an additional N-terminal tyrosine. Products advertised as Fragment 176–191 are frequently discussed using those neighboring compounds’ evidence. This profile remains separate from AOD-9604 so that uncertainty is visible instead of silently merging unlike identities. There is no established clinical obesity treatment defined solely by the phrase 'HGH fragment.' Exact sequence, modification, purity and the actual studied material are prerequisites for a valid evidence comparison.
mechanism: Research on C-terminal growth-hormone sequences explored whether effects on lipid synthesis could be separated from the full hormone’s growth-promoting actions. A study of hGH 177–191 found an antilipogenic effect in rats but did not find significant stimulation of lipolysis under its test conditions. That distinction matters: less synthesis of fat is not the same mechanism as increased breakdown, and neither automatically establishes human weight reduction.
keyTakeaway: Fragment 176–191 should be treated as an identity-sensitive research entry. Neither related animal findings nor AOD-9604’s clinical history establish safe, effective human fat loss for an ambiguously labeled fragment product.

sections.title: Why the names are not automatically aliases
sections.body: The analytical literature defines AOD-9604 as hGH residues 177–191 with added tyrosine. That is a specific modified molecule. A reference to native residues or a nonspecific fragment label does not by itself prove the same identity.

sections.title: What the original fragment experiment measured
sections.body: The 1993 study examined a synthetic 177–191 sequence in rats. It reported inhibition of lipid synthesis but no significant lipolytic effect by its glycerol-release measurement. It was neither a human obesity trial nor direct proof for every 176–191 product.

sections.title: Can AOD-9604 results be borrowed?
sections.body: Only with explicit identification of the molecule and an appropriate scientific rationale. Moreover, AOD-9604’s larger obesity trial failed to show significant benefit over placebo, so borrowing its evidence would not establish a proven human weight-loss treatment anyway.

sections.title: What is not established
sections.body: A fragment lacking selected intact-GH activities is not automatically harmless. Route-specific human exposure, endocrine effects, immune responses and long-term toxicity remain insufficiently characterized for products sold under this broad label.

sections.title: How to interpret a vendor description
sections.body: A claim that the product contains the 'fat-burning part' of growth hormone compresses identity, mechanism and clinical efficacy into one unsupported conclusion. The knowledge record keeps those questions separate and does not infer an approved indication from a sequence nickname.

name: Albiglutide
molecularClass: GLP-1 analog fused to human albumin
summary: Albiglutide is a long-acting GLP-1 medicine previously marketed for type 2 diabetes. It has randomized cardiovascular-outcome evidence, but its historical approvals must be distinguished from current availability: the European authorization was withdrawn after commercial discontinuation.
description: Albiglutide was marketed as Tanzeum in the United States and Eperzan in Europe. Its albumin-fusion design prolonged GLP-1 activity and supported weekly injection for adult type 2 diabetes. The HARMONY Outcomes study later demonstrated cardiovascular benefit in a high-risk diabetes population. Despite that clinical record, the manufacturer discontinued marketing, and the European Commission withdrew the Eperzan authorization in 2018 at the company’s request for commercial reasons. This profile preserves the evidence and approval history without implying that a currently obtainable albiglutide product is a routine treatment option in every market.
mechanism: The molecule joins modified GLP-1 sequences to human albumin, extending circulation time and protecting activity compared with native GLP-1. Receptor activation increases glucose-dependent insulin release, reduces inappropriate glucagon secretion and affects gastric emptying. Albumin fusion changes exposure and delivery but does not remove the physiological consequences of GLP-1 signaling, including gastrointestinal adverse effects and interactions with other glucose-lowering treatment.
keyTakeaway: Albiglutide is clinically important as an established GLP-1 research and treatment history, but a historical approval is not evidence of current supply. Its withdrawal and cardiovascular trial findings should both remain visible.

sections.title: Original approved indication
sections.body: The original FDA label approved albiglutide with diet and exercise for glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. It was not an approved type 1 diabetes or obesity medicine.

sections.title: Cardiovascular findings
sections.body: HARMONY Outcomes enrolled patients with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease and found fewer major cardiovascular events with albiglutide than placebo. This later trial is more informative about cardiovascular efficacy than the older initial label’s statement that outcomes evidence was not yet available.

sections.title: Known adverse effects
sections.body: The historical label identifies gastrointestinal symptoms and injection-site reactions, with warnings about pancreatitis, serious allergy and hypoglycemia when combined with insulin or insulin secretagogues. Medullary thyroid carcinoma history and MEN2 were contraindications.

sections.title: Why the withdrawal matters
sections.body: EMA states that the European Commission withdrew Eperzan’s authorization on 29 October 2018 after the manufacturer permanently discontinued marketing for commercial reasons. That is different from claiming a demonstrated new safety failure caused the withdrawal.

sections.title: How this record should be used
sections.body: The article supports understanding of the GLP-1 class and historical evidence. It does not establish that an online albiglutide listing is an authorized or available replacement for a currently marketed diabetes medicine.

name: Corticotropin
summary: Corticotropin is the ACTH hormone signal used therapeutically in specific repository preparations, including infantile spasms and selected inflammatory disorders. It stimulates adrenal steroid production and has substantial steroid-like risks, including infection, metabolic effects and adrenal suppression after prolonged treatment.
description: Repository corticotropin injection, such as Acthar Gel, is a pharmaceutical ACTH-based preparation with specific indications and formulation requirements. Its label includes monotherapy for infantile spasms in children under two and treatment of adult multiple-sclerosis exacerbations, as well as selected rheumatic, dermatologic, ophthalmic and other disorders. These indications do not make corticotropin a general adrenal-support product. It is also distinct from cosyntropin, the shorter synthetic ACTH fragment used primarily for diagnostic adrenal stimulation. The same hormonal pathway can be used therapeutically or diagnostically, with very different exposure and risk.
mechanism: ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce corticosteroids, including cortisol, through melanocortin-2 receptor signaling. Corticotropin preparations may interact with additional melanocortin pathways, but the mechanism for every therapeutic indication is not fully established. Increased endogenous steroid exposure explains many recognized effects, including immune suppression, fluid retention, glucose disturbance and suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis during prolonged treatment.
keyTakeaway: Corticotropin is a potent prescription therapy with selected established indications, not nonspecific hormone optimization. Its benefits must be weighed against steroid-related complications and the consequences of stopping prolonged treatment.

sections.title: Indication and formulation matter
sections.body: Infantile-spasm treatment uses the specifically labeled preparation and route; the adult self-injector presentation is not labeled for this pediatric use. The wide historical indication list still requires a disease-specific rationale rather than assuming benefit for any inflammatory symptom.

sections.title: Evidence in infantile spasms
sections.body: A small randomized blinded study assessed both cessation of spasms and resolution of the characteristic EEG abnormality. ACTH outperformed the prednisone regimen used in that study. The comparison is regimen-specific and should not be generalized to all modern steroid approaches.

sections.title: Infection and metabolic risks
sections.body: The label warns about increased susceptibility to infection, Cushing-like effects, hypertension, fluid retention, low potassium, gastrointestinal bleeding, mood changes and worsening diabetes. Prolonged therapy can suppress adrenal function, with risk after withdrawal.

sections.title: Important contraindications
sections.body: Examples include systemic fungal infection, uncontrolled hypertension, heart failure, primary adrenal insufficiency and certain other conditions. Live vaccines are contraindicated during immunosuppressive exposure. Porcine-protein sensitivity and serious hypersensitivity to the product also matter.

sections.title: Therapy versus a diagnostic ACTH test
sections.body: Therapeutic repository corticotropin creates sustained hormonal exposure. A cosyntropin stimulation test uses a different molecule and purpose to assess adrenal reserve. Evidence and safety from a short diagnostic test cannot be transferred to repeated corticotropin treatment.

name: Cosyntropin
summary: Cosyntropin is a synthetic ACTH fragment used to test adrenal cortisol reserve. It is an approved diagnostic agent, not routine long-term treatment for fatigue or low cortisol, and test interpretation depends on medications, cortisol-binding proteins and the clinical setting.
description: Cortrosyn contains the first twenty-four amino acids of ACTH, which retain the adrenal-stimulating activity needed for a diagnostic challenge. Clinicians measure cortisol responses in conjunction with other information when investigating possible adrenal insufficiency. A result must be interpreted with the assay, timing, illness context and the suspected location of a hormonal defect in mind. The current label specifically addresses misleading cortisol values from medicines and altered cortisol-binding globulin. A single stimulated total-cortisol measurement therefore should not be treated as a complete explanation for chronic tiredness or every suspected endocrine disorder.
mechanism: Cosyntropin activates ACTH receptors on adrenal cortical cells and stimulates steroid synthesis, including cortisol. Measuring the resulting cortisol response tests the adrenal gland’s capacity to respond to that stimulus. It does not directly measure every aspect of hypothalamic or pituitary function. Total cortisol is also affected by binding proteins, so a change in measured concentration can reflect more than adrenal steroid production alone.
keyTakeaway: Cosyntropin is a useful diagnostic tool when performed and interpreted in context. The assay, medications, binding proteins and clinical suspicion determine what its cortisol response can reliably establish.

sections.title: Approved diagnostic role
sections.body: The current U.S. label authorizes use with other diagnostic tests to screen for adrenocortical insufficiency in adults and children. It does not authorize general hormone enhancement or ongoing adrenal replacement.

sections.title: Why assay and context matter
sections.body: The response is one component of an endocrine assessment. Laboratory methods and clinical circumstances influence the threshold used to judge adequacy, while the distinction between primary adrenal disease and central causes may require additional information.

sections.title: Medicines can distort the result
sections.body: Glucocorticoids, spironolactone and estrogen-containing drugs can affect cortisol measurement or cortisol-binding globulin. The label provides test-preparation considerations, which should be managed by the testing clinician rather than through unsupervised medication changes.

sections.title: Adverse reactions and protein binding
sections.body: Hypersensitivity, including anaphylaxis, has been reported and is an important immediate risk. Cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome and other states altering cortisol-binding globulin can produce misleading total cortisol levels without a corresponding change in biologically active hormone.

sections.title: Why it differs from corticotropin therapy
sections.body: Cosyntropin is a short synthetic fragment used as a diagnostic stimulus. Repository corticotropin is used therapeutically for selected diseases. Sharing ACTH activity does not make the products interchangeable or transfer their indications and long-term safety assumptions.

name: Dulaglutide
summary: Dulaglutide is an approved weekly GLP-1 medicine for type 2 diabetes from age ten and for cardiovascular risk reduction in defined adults with diabetes. It has substantial outcomes evidence, but it is not an FDA-approved chronic weight-management product.
description: Trulicity contains dulaglutide, a long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist designed for weekly subcutaneous use. Its U.S. indication includes glycemic control in adults and children aged ten and older with type 2 diabetes. A separate adult indication reduces major cardiovascular events in people with established cardiovascular disease or multiple risk factors. The latter is broader than requiring a prior cardiovascular event, reflecting the REWIND trial population. Weight changes may accompany treatment, but that observation should not be rewritten as an obesity indication or a reason to combine it with another GLP-1 medicine.
mechanism: Dulaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors, increasing beta-cell cyclic AMP and glucose-dependent insulin release. It also reduces glucagon secretion and delays gastric emptying. Fusion-protein engineering prolongs its exposure. The glucose-dependent mechanism reduces, but does not abolish, hypoglycemia concerns; risk becomes more important when insulin or insulin secretagogues are also part of the treatment regimen.
keyTakeaway: Dulaglutide is established diabetes and cardiovascular-risk care for its labeled populations. Its evidence should be matched to diabetes status and cardiovascular risk, with gastrointestinal and endocrine precautions kept in view.

sections.title: Current label boundaries
sections.body: The diabetes indication includes adults and children ten or older. Cardiovascular risk reduction applies to adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors. It is not a type 1 diabetes treatment.

sections.title: What REWIND contributes
sections.body: REWIND showed fewer major cardiovascular events with dulaglutide than placebo in adults with type 2 diabetes, including many without a previous event. This supports the risk-factor-based label and should be distinguished from trials restricted to secondary prevention.

sections.title: Major adverse effects and exclusions
sections.body: Gastrointestinal symptoms are common. Pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, dehydration-related kidney injury and serious allergy are recognized concerns. A personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 is a contraindication related to the thyroid C-cell tumor warning.

sections.title: Other clinical considerations
sections.body: The label addresses diabetic retinopathy complications, severe gastroparesis and aspiration during anesthesia or deep sedation. Glucose monitoring becomes especially relevant with concurrent insulin or secretagogues, while dehydration can increase kidney risk.

sections.title: Does weekly delivery mean identical GLP-1 effects?
sections.body: No. Each medicine has its own molecule, exposure, approved populations and outcomes trials. Dulaglutide’s cardiovascular evidence should not be assigned to every GLP-1 product, and another product’s weight-management approval does not extend to Trulicity.

name: Exenatide
summary: Exenatide is an approved GLP-1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes, available in distinct immediate- and extended-release formulations. Its kidney considerations, rare immune-mediated thrombocytopenia and formulation-specific restrictions make it important to consult the actual product label.
description: Exenatide was among the early GLP-1 medicines and is based on the exendin-4 peptide sequence. Shorter-acting products and extended-release microsphere products differ in exposure, eligibility and adverse-effect profiles. Brand discontinuation in a market should also be distinguished from the existence of a current generic or another formulation: a 2026 DailyMed label describes immediate-release exenatide injection. The medicine is used to improve glycemic control in type 2 diabetes, not as an established obesity drug or substitute for insulin in type 1 diabetes. The formulation is therefore part of the clinical identity, not a minor packaging detail.
mechanism: Exenatide activates GLP-1 receptors and promotes insulin release when glucose is elevated, reduces inappropriate glucagon secretion and slows gastric emptying. It resists rapid breakdown by DPP-4 compared with native GLP-1. Renal clearance contributes to its exposure, which is one reason kidney function and dehydration matter. Sustained-release technology changes the duration of delivery without changing the underlying receptor target.
keyTakeaway: Exenatide is established diabetes therapy, but its formulations are not interchangeable by name alone. Kidney status, gastrointestinal tolerance, immune reactions and the current product’s specific instructions determine safe clinical use.

sections.title: Formulation-specific populations
sections.body: The current immediate-release generic label covers adult type 2 diabetes with diet and exercise. Extended-release labeling differs, including its pediatric population and additional precautions. One formulation’s label should not be used as a shortcut for another.

sections.title: What established efficacy means
sections.body: Registration studies demonstrate improved glycemic control in the specified diabetes settings. A reduction in HbA1c or body weight is not equivalent to proven benefit for unrelated neurologic diseases or to approval as a chronic obesity treatment.

sections.title: Important adverse effects
sections.body: Nausea and other gastrointestinal effects can lead to dehydration and kidney injury. Pancreatitis, gallbladder disease and serious hypersensitivity are recognized. Rare drug-induced immune-mediated thrombocytopenia can cause serious bleeding and is a contraindication to re-exposure when it has occurred.

sections.title: Kidney function and concurrent treatment
sections.body: The product label includes renal limitations and cautions. Insulin and insulin secretagogues increase hypoglycemia risk. Antibody formation can affect response, and persistent deterioration in glycemic control requires clinical reassessment rather than assuming inadequate appetite suppression.

sections.title: Why older brand information can mislead
sections.body: A historical brand listing does not establish current availability, and a brand withdrawal does not necessarily mean the ingredient lacks any approved presentation. The current authorized formulation and its label are the appropriate reference for clinical decisions.

name: Insulin analogs (multiple)
molecularClass: Engineered insulin peptide hormones; multiple distinct medicines
summary: Insulin analogs are a family of essential diabetes medicines engineered to provide meal-related or sustained insulin activity. They have extensive clinical evidence, but differ in action profile, concentration, delivery device and approved use; medication mix-ups or inappropriate substitution can cause dangerous glucose changes.
description: This family includes rapid-acting analogs such as lispro, aspart and glulisine, and basal analogs such as glargine and degludec; detemir is another established basal analog. Each product has its own formulation, concentration and delivery compatibility. Insulin replaces or supplements a hormone that is essential for glucose regulation, particularly in type 1 diabetes. It is not a general muscle-building or anti-aging peptide. A family-level overview can explain common biology, but treatment decisions require the exact insulin, device, monitoring information and clinical context.
mechanism: Insulin binds the insulin receptor and promotes glucose uptake in muscle and fat while suppressing hepatic glucose production. It also affects protein and lipid metabolism and shifts potassium into cells. Amino-acid changes and formulation technologies alter absorption and duration, producing meal-time or basal profiles. These pharmacokinetic differences are clinically consequential even though the medicines share the same fundamental receptor pathway.
keyTakeaway: Insulin analogs are established, potentially lifesaving medicines whose differences matter. The specific product, concentration and delivery system must remain visible; a generic peptide label is not enough to guide substitution or use.

sections.title: Basal and meal-related roles
sections.body: Basal insulin provides background action, while rapid-acting formulations address meal-related needs or other specifically prescribed roles. Pump, intravenous and subcutaneous permissions vary by product and concentration; they are not universal properties of every insulin analog.

sections.title: How benefit is evaluated
sections.body: Insulin trials assess glycemic control and hypoglycemia alongside practical treatment performance. A useful regimen balances glucose exposure against low-glucose events, rather than pursuing a single laboratory target without regard to safety and daily function.

sections.title: Acute and local adverse effects
sections.body: Hypoglycemia can be life-threatening. Potassium shifts can cause hypokalemia, and serious allergy can occur. Repeated use at the same site can produce lipodystrophy or localized amyloid deposits, altering absorption and glucose response.

sections.title: Why concentration and device must be explicit
sections.body: Different concentrations and pen systems create medication-error risks. Product labels warn against sharing pens and require particular handling when changing regimens. A nominal volume or a syringe marking is not a universal insulin-dose equivalence.

sections.title: What a family record cannot replace
sections.body: Meal patterns, physical activity, kidney or liver impairment and other medicines can change insulin requirements. This overview deliberately supplies pharmacology and safety context rather than an individualized regimen; the exact medicine and glucose data are necessary for prescribing decisions.

name: Lixisenatide
summary: Lixisenatide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist used for adult type 2 diabetes, including in a fixed combination with insulin glargine. It has a prominent effect on gastric emptying, and its cardiovascular trial demonstrated safety without establishing a cardiovascular-event reduction advantage.
description: The standalone medicine was approved as Adlyxin, while Soliqua 100/33 combines lixisenatide with basal insulin glargine. These products must be distinguished because the combination adds insulin’s hypoglycemia and medication-error risks. Current DailyMed information confirms the combination’s adult type 2 diabetes indication. Lixisenatide is not an approved obesity treatment or a replacement for insulin in type 1 diabetes. Its place in diabetes care depends on the actual product, renal function, gastrointestinal tolerance and the broader regimen rather than the assumption that all GLP-1 agents have identical outcome evidence.
mechanism: Lixisenatide activates GLP-1 receptors to support glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress inappropriate glucagon release and delay gastric emptying. The gastric effect contributes to control of post-meal glucose but can also change absorption of oral medicines. In a fixed insulin-glargine combination, the two components address different parts of glycemic control; the combination is not equivalent to lixisenatide alone.
keyTakeaway: Lixisenatide is established diabetes pharmacology with product-specific use. Its combination with insulin and its neutral cardiovascular-outcome trial should remain explicit when comparing it with other incretin medicines.

sections.title: Standalone and combination roles
sections.body: Adlyxin’s label covers adult type 2 diabetes. Soliqua is also an adult diabetes product but contains both insulin and lixisenatide. The combination is not recommended for diabetic ketoacidosis and has not been studied with prandial insulin.

sections.title: Cardiovascular trial interpretation
sections.body: ELIXA studied patients with type 2 diabetes after a recent acute coronary event. Lixisenatide was noninferior to placebo for the cardiovascular safety endpoint, but did not show superiority. This should not be rewritten as the cardiovascular benefit demonstrated by some other GLP-1 medicines.

sections.title: Adverse effects and kidney considerations
sections.body: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and other gastrointestinal symptoms are common. Pancreatitis, serious allergy, gallbladder disease and dehydration-related kidney injury are label concerns. Severe gastroparesis and end-stage renal disease require particular attention to product restrictions.

sections.title: Gastric emptying and oral medicines
sections.body: Delayed gastric emptying can alter the timing of oral-drug exposure. The label contains specific considerations for medicines whose prompt absorption matters, including some contraceptives. Anesthesia teams also need to know about GLP-1 treatment because of aspiration concerns.

sections.title: What changes when insulin is included?
sections.body: The fixed combination introduces basal-insulin activity and its associated hypoglycemia risk. Device settings, product limits and switching instructions belong to that combination’s label; they cannot be inferred from a standalone lixisenatide description.

name: Mecasermin
molecularClass: Recombinant human insulin-like growth factor-1 protein
summary: Mecasermin is an approved IGF-1 replacement medicine for specific severe pediatric growth disorders. It is not interchangeable with growth hormone and is not an approved bodybuilding or anti-aging therapy; hypoglycemia, tissue overgrowth and malignancy-related precautions are central to its use.
description: Increlex treats growth failure in children aged two and older with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, or growth-hormone gene deletion with neutralizing antibodies to GH. Primary IGF-1 deficiency means the problem is not simply inadequate GH secretion. The label excludes common secondary causes such as malnutrition, hypothyroidism or conventional GH deficiency. Diagnosis therefore determines whether replacing IGF-1 is biologically appropriate. Open growth plates and absence of prohibited malignancy history also matter. A low IGF-1 laboratory value alone does not establish this indication or justify use to improve strength in adults.
mechanism: IGF-1 mediates many growth-promoting effects normally stimulated by GH. Mecasermin directly activates the IGF-1 receptor, supporting cell growth and uptake of glucose, amino acids and fatty acids. Direct administration bypasses the need for GH to generate adequate IGF-1, which can be useful in selected GH-resistant conditions. Its insulin-like metabolic actions also explain the possibility of severe hypoglycemia.
keyTakeaway: Mecasermin is a targeted pediatric replacement therapy for defined IGF-1 disorders. Its indication cannot be inferred from short stature or a single low test result, and its growth and glucose effects require specialist monitoring.

sections.title: Who qualifies
sections.body: The label covers severe primary IGF-1 deficiency or GH gene deletion with neutralizing GH antibodies. It specifically states that mecasermin is not a substitute for GH in approved GH indications and is not for secondary IGF-1 deficiency from malnutrition or hypothyroidism.

sections.title: What treatment studies assess
sections.body: Long-term clinical work evaluated growth in children with severe IGF-1 deficiency. Height velocity and attained growth are the relevant outcomes. This evidence does not establish improved athletic performance, adult muscle gain or lifespan extension.

sections.title: Glucose and tissue-growth risks
sections.body: Severe hypoglycemia can occur. Other important concerns include intracranial hypertension, enlarged tonsils or adenoids, slipped capital femoral epiphysis and progression of scoliosis. Serious allergic reactions are possible.

sections.title: Growth plates and malignancy
sections.body: Mecasermin is contraindicated for growth promotion after epiphyseal closure and in pediatric patients with malignant neoplasia or a history of malignancy. The label calls for discontinuation if evidence of malignant disease develops.

sections.title: IGF-1 and GH are different treatments
sections.body: GH acts upstream to stimulate IGF-1 production; mecasermin supplies IGF-1 directly. The correct treatment depends on where the growth pathway is impaired, so one hormone cannot be substituted for the other based solely on a desire to raise a laboratory value.

name: Pasireotide
summary: Pasireotide is an approved somatostatin analog for selected pituitary hormone-excess disorders. It can reduce ACTH-driven cortisol production in Cushing’s disease and, in its long-acting formulation, treat acromegaly, but hyperglycemia and diabetes are prominent treatment concerns.
description: Signifor and Signifor LAR contain pasireotide with different delivery profiles. The immediate-release product is approved for adults with Cushing’s disease when pituitary surgery is unsuitable or not curative. The depot product also has an acromegaly indication after inadequate surgery or when surgery is not an option. Cushing’s disease specifically refers to pituitary ACTH-driven cortisol excess and should not be confused with every form of Cushing’s syndrome. The desired hormonal response can improve illness while simultaneously creating new metabolic problems, so benefit is assessed together with glucose control and other safety measures.
mechanism: Pasireotide binds several somatostatin receptor subtypes, with strong activity at SSTR5, which is frequently expressed by corticotroph pituitary tumors. Suppressing ACTH can lower adrenal cortisol secretion. In acromegaly, inhibition of GH secretion reduces downstream IGF-1. Its broader receptor profile differs from octreotide and lanreotide, and suppression of insulin-related pathways contributes to the notable hyperglycemia risk.
keyTakeaway: Pasireotide is a specialist option for selected pituitary disease, with a meaningful tradeoff between hormone control and metabolic toxicity. Product formulation, cortisol or IGF-1 response and glucose monitoring must be considered together.

sections.title: Disease and formulation boundaries
sections.body: Cushing’s disease treatment is aimed at a pituitary source of ACTH excess. The long-acting formulation also treats specified acromegaly populations. Neither is a general treatment for stress-associated cortisol variation or an unexplained abnormal hormone test.

sections.title: Cortisol-control evidence
sections.body: The pivotal Cushing’s study assessed urinary free cortisol and clinical changes. Some patients achieved biochemical control, but response was not universal and was influenced by baseline disease severity. That supports monitored treatment rather than an expectation of guaranteed normalization.

sections.title: Metabolic and cardiac concerns
sections.body: Hyperglycemia may appear soon after initiation and can require diabetes treatment. The labels also address bradycardia, QT prolongation, liver-test abnormalities, gallstones and gastrointestinal symptoms. Excess cortisol suppression can produce adrenal insufficiency.

sections.title: Assessing both benefit and burden
sections.body: Glucose, HbA1c, liver tests, ECG-related risk and electrolytes are relevant before and during therapy. Hormone response and symptoms are followed alongside adverse effects. New steatorrhea or weight loss can indicate pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.

sections.title: Why somatostatin analogs differ
sections.body: Pasireotide, lanreotide and octreotide share a family relationship but have different receptor profiles and approved roles. One agent’s glucose effects or tumor evidence should not be assumed for another, and depot formulations require their own prescribing instructions.

name: Pegvisomant
summary: Pegvisomant is an approved medicine that blocks growth-hormone action in acromegaly. Unlike GH replacement or GH-releasing peptides, it reduces downstream IGF-1 signaling; follow-up emphasizes IGF-1, liver function, glucose and the underlying pituitary tumor rather than GH concentration alone.
description: Somavert is used in acromegaly when surgery or radiotherapy has been inadequate or is unsuitable. The medicine acts outside the pituitary by blocking GH receptors in target tissues, so it can reduce IGF-1 even when GH secretion remains elevated. That distinction explains why biochemical monitoring differs from treatment that suppresses hormone release. Pegvisomant does not directly remove a pituitary tumor, and ongoing assessment of the underlying lesion remains part of care. It is not a peptide for increasing growth, athletic performance or muscle mass; its intended action is to oppose excessive GH signaling.
mechanism: Pegvisomant is an engineered GH analog with polyethylene-glycol modification that binds the GH receptor without producing normal receptor activation. It competitively blocks endogenous GH signaling, reducing hepatic and tissue responses including IGF-1 production. This may improve insulin sensitivity in patients with GH excess. Standard GH measurements can be misleading during treatment because pegvisomant may interfere with assays and does not suppress secretion in the same way as pituitary-directed drugs.
keyTakeaway: Pegvisomant treats excess GH action by blocking its receptor. A falling IGF-1 can show benefit even without a falling GH result, while liver safety, glucose changes and pituitary follow-up remain necessary.

sections.title: Where it fits in acromegaly care
sections.body: The label covers patients with inadequate response to surgery or radiation, or for whom these treatments are inappropriate. The goal is normalization of IGF-1, rather than use for nonspecific symptoms attributed to hormone imbalance.

sections.title: Receptor-blockade efficacy
sections.body: A randomized trial demonstrated dose-related reduction and normalization of IGF-1 in acromegaly. This established the ability to block peripheral GH effects, a different therapeutic strategy from inhibiting GH secretion at the pituitary.

sections.title: Liver and injection-site effects
sections.body: Liver enzyme elevations and liver injury require attention to label-based monitoring. Systemic hypersensitivity and injection-site changes, including lipohypertrophy, can occur. Improved insulin sensitivity may increase hypoglycemia risk in patients receiving glucose-lowering medicines.

sections.title: Why GH is not the response target
sections.body: The label directs assessment using IGF-1. GH assay interference and ongoing endogenous GH secretion make GH concentration unsuitable as the sole efficacy marker. Monitoring of pituitary tumor size remains relevant because receptor blockade is not direct tumor removal.

sections.title: Opposite direction from GH replacement
sections.body: Somatropin supplies GH activity, while pegvisomant blocks it. Their structural relationship does not imply similar therapeutic goals. A peptide catalog should preserve that opposite action rather than grouping both under an undifferentiated growth-hormone benefit.
